items.title: The Slow Clock
items.question: Two identical clocks start together. One stays on Earth, the other flies around the world and returns. When reunited, what do they read?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — moving clocks tick slower, so the journeying timepiece returns younger.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the travelled clock lags behind. Velocity dilates time, so the flying clock accumulates fewer seconds. Hafele and Keating proved it with atomic clocks on airliners.
items.lessonContent:
Velocity dilates time: the faster you move, the slower your clock ticks relative to home.
Airplane atomic clocks landed measurably younger than their twins.
GPS satellites must correct for this daily or drift kilometres off.
The effect is tiny at human speeds and enormous near light speed.
Share this: explain tonight why frequent flyers age — very slightly — slower.

items.title: Twins Reunited
items.question: One twin rockets away near light speed and returns. Which twin is older at reunion?
items.correctExplanation: Right — the travelling twin accelerated and turned, breaking the symmetry; less time passes for them.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the travelling twin is younger. Only one twin turns around, so only one changes inertial frames — that asymmetry resolves the paradox. Cruise-phase symmetry fools intuition; the turnaround decides it.
items.lessonContent:
Acceleration breaks the symmetry: only one twin turns around.
Each sees the other's clock slow during cruise — both views are valid.
The turnaround is what makes their histories genuinely different.
No paradox survives careful bookkeeping of who accelerated.
Share this: ask someone which twin ages less, then name the turnaround.

items.title: The Cosmic Limit
items.question: No matter how hard you push a spaceship, what can it never reach?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — adding energy near light speed adds momentum more than velocity; massive objects asymptote below it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: light speed with mass aboard. Each push buys less speed and more momentum as the limit nears. Only massless things ride exactly at the limit; everything else approaches it forever.
items.lessonContent:
Adding energy near light speed adds momentum more than velocity.
Massive objects asymptote: ever closer, never arriving.
Only massless things ride exactly at the limit.
The limit is really about causality, not engines.
Share this: explain tonight why the limit is a speed, not a place.

items.title: Valley Clocks
items.question: Two perfect clocks start synced. One descends to a deep valley, the other stays on the peak. A year later, which lags?
choices: The peak clock, worn by weather
items.correctExplanation: Right — gravity dilates time: deeper in a gravitational well, slower the ticking.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the lower clock runs slower. Pound and Rebka measured the effect across a mere building. Your head ages faster than your feet — by billionths of a second. GPS must subtract this daily or drift.
items.lessonContent:
Gravity dilates time: deeper in a well, slower the ticking.
Pound and Rebka measured the effect across a mere building.
Your head ages faster than your feet — by billionths of a second.
GPS must subtract this daily or drift.
Share this: tell someone their head is older than their feet, technically.

items.title: Every Observer Agrees
items.question: What does every observer measure for the speed of light in vacuum, regardless of their own motion?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — light's speed never adds to yours; invariance anchors all of relativity.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the same for everyone. Chasing a beam at half light speed, you still clock it full. Everything strange — dilation, contraction — flows from this one fact. Michelson and Morley found it hunting something else entirely.
items.lessonContent:
Invariance anchors relativity: light's speed never adds to yours.
Chasing a beam at half light speed, you still clock it full.
Everything strange — dilation, contraction — flows from this one fact.
Michelson and Morley found it by accident, hunting something else.
Share this: ask someone what happens when you chase light at near its pace.

items.title: Whose Now?
items.question: Two lightning strikes hit opposite ends of a moving train. Ground observers call them simultaneous. What do passengers say?
items.correctExplanation: Right — simultaneity is frame-bound: 'at the same time' needs a stated viewpoint.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: they disagree about simultaneity. Einstein's train made the point with two lightning bolts. No view is privileged; each is fully consistent. Distant 'nows' are conventions, not facts.
items.lessonContent:
Simultaneity is frame-bound: 'at the same time' needs a stated viewpoint.
Einstein's train made the point with two lightning bolts.
No view is privileged; each is fully consistent.
Distant 'nows' are conventions, not facts.
Share this: ask whether aliens are acting 'now' — then dismantle the question.

items.title: The Bent Stage
items.question: In general relativity, what is gravity?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — mass tells the stage how to bend; the bent stage tells matter how to move.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: curved spacetime. Orbits are straight lines drawn on a curved surface. The image replaces invisible ropes with pure geometry. Apples and moons obey the same curvature.
items.lessonContent:
Mass tells the stage how to bend; the bent stage tells matter how to move.
Orbits are straight lines drawn on a curved surface.
The image replaces invisible ropes with pure geometry.
Apples and moons obey the same curvature.
Share this: roll a marble across a stretched sheet with a weight in the middle.

items.title: The Restless Orbit
items.question: Which planet's orbit famously refused to fit Newton's predictions until relativity explained it?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Newton missed a tiny extra swivel in Mercury's orbit; curved geometry predicted it exactly.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Mercury, the swift messenger. Astronomers hunted a hidden planet, Vulcan, in vain. Einstein's curved geometry predicted the swivel exactly. The 1919 eclipse sealed the new picture.
items.lessonContent:
Newton's math missed a tiny extra swivel — arcseconds per century.
Astronomers hunted a hidden planet, Vulcan, in vain.
Einstein's curved geometry predicted the swivel exactly.
The 1919 eclipse sealed the new picture.
Share this: explain tonight how a wobble smaller than a coin at arm's length rewrote physics.

items.title: Frozen Energy
items.question: What does E = mc² fundamentally claim?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — a little mass converts to enormous energy because c² is huge.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: mass is frozen energy. The Sun spends mass like income to shine. Nuclear reactions audit the books: the missing mass left as energy. Matter is not stuff plus energy — it is energy, bound.
items.lessonContent:
A little mass converts to enormous energy because c² is huge.
The Sun spends mass like income to shine.
Nuclear reactions audit the books: the missing mass left as energy.
Matter is not stuff plus energy — it is energy, bound.
Share this: compute the energy hiding in one paperclip tonight.

items.title: The Long-Lived Muon
items.question: Muons created high in the atmosphere decay in microseconds, yet reach the ground. What saves them?
items.correctExplanation: Right — fast motion stretches internal clocks: the traveler's own seconds last longer at home.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: time-stretched lifespans. From our view the particles live extended lives and complete the trip. From theirs, the atmosphere contracts to a thin sheet. Both accounts agree on the detector clicks.
items.lessonContent:
Fast motion stretches internal clocks: the traveler's own seconds last longer at home.
From our view the particles live extended lives and complete the trip.
From theirs, the atmosphere contracts to a thin sheet.
Both accounts agree on the detector clicks.
Share this: explain tonight why fast things get extra time — from our side.

items.title: Satellite Seconds
items.question: Why must GPS satellites correct their clocks daily?
choices: Speed slows them, low gravity quickens them
items.correctAnswer: Speed slows them, low gravity quickens them
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — velocity dilates while weaker gravity undoes more; the net gain is microseconds a day.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: speed slows them, low gravity quickens them. Two effects tug satellite time opposite ways. The net gain is microseconds a day — kilometres of error uncorrected. Every phone quietly runs relativity to find itself.
items.lessonContent:
Two effects tug satellite time opposite ways.
Speed dilates; weaker gravity undoes more.
The net gain is microseconds a day — kilometres of error uncorrected.
Every phone quietly runs relativity to find itself.
Share this: tell someone their map app audits Einstein before breakfast.

items.title: Whose Moment?
items.question: Can two distant events share one single moment?
items.correctExplanation: Right — distant simultaneity is a convention, not a discovery; physics keeps causality strict while letting 'now' dissolve.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: no absolute simultaneity exists. Andromeda's 'now' shifts by days depending on whether you stroll toward it. The block universe pictures all moments equally real. Physics keeps causality strict while letting 'now' dissolve.
items.lessonContent:
Distant simultaneity is a convention, not a discovery.
Andromeda's 'now' shifts by days depending on whether you stroll toward it.
The block universe pictures all moments equally real.
Physics keeps causality strict while letting 'now' dissolve.
Share this: ask whether aliens are acting 'now' — then dismantle the question.

items.title: The Squeezed Ruler
items.question: What happens to a fast-moving object's length along its direction of motion?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — motion squeezes length along the travel direction only.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: it contracts. Transverse dimensions never notice the speed. At everyday paces the squeezing is absurdly below detection. Only near light speed does the ruler visibly shorten.
items.lessonContent:
Motion squeezes length along the travel direction only.
Transverse dimensions never notice the speed.
At everyday paces the squeezing is absurdly below detection.
Only near light speed does the ruler visibly shorten.
Share this: explain tonight why a near-light spaceship looks like a pancake.

items.title: No Return Address
items.question: Why can nothing ever leave a black hole — not even the fastest signal?
choices: Its gravity pulls too hard to climb
Leaving would need exceeding light speed
items.correctAnswer: Leaving would need exceeding light speed
items.correctExplanation: Right — at the horizon that speed passes light's — and nothing outruns light.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: leaving would need exceeding light speed. Escape velocity is the speed a projectile needs to leave forever. Inside, all futures point inward; outward is the past. The boundary is one-way by geometry, not by force.
items.lessonContent:
Escape velocity is the speed a projectile needs to leave forever.
At the horizon that speed passes light's — and nothing outruns light.
Inside, all futures point inward; outward is the past.
The boundary is one-way by geometry, not by force.
Share this: explain tonight why 'too strong a pull' is the wrong picture.

items.title: The One-Way Boundary
items.question: What marks the edge of a black hole?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — cross it and every path leads inward; return needs a time machine.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the event horizon. Outside observers never see the crossing; time appears to freeze at the edge. The boundary's size scales directly with mass. Inside, the singularity is less a place than a future moment.
items.lessonContent:
Cross it and every path leads inward — return needs a time machine.
Outside observers never see the crossing; time appears to freeze at the edge.
The boundary's size scales directly with mass.
Inside, the singularity is less a place than a future moment.
Share this: tell someone the edge is defined by geometry, not by a wall.

items.title: Ripples in Reality
items.question: What did LIGO detect in 2015?
items.correctExplanation: Right — two dead stars spiraled together, shaking spacetime itself.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: merging black holes. The ripple squeezed Earth by less than a proton's width — and we heard it. A century after prediction, the wave arrived on schedule. Astronomy gained ears to match its eyes.
items.lessonContent:
Two dead stars spiraled together, shaking spacetime itself.
The ripple squeezed Earth by less than a proton's width — and we heard it.
A century after prediction, the wave arrived on schedule.
Astronomy gained ears to match its eyes.
Share this: explain tonight that we now listen to the universe, not just look.

items.title: The Eclipse Proof
items.question: During the 1919 eclipse, starlight near the Sun appeared in the wrong place. What did that prove?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — starlight grazing the Sun arrived displaced; the sky itself was lensed.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: mass bends light. Eddington's teams measured the shift on photographic plates. Headlines made Einstein a celebrity overnight. The bending matched curved geometry to the arcsecond.
items.lessonContent:
Starlight grazing the Sun arrived displaced — the sky itself was lensed.
Eddington's teams measured the shift on photographic plates.
Headlines made Einstein a celebrity overnight.
The bending matched curved geometry to the arcsecond.
Share this: tell someone the most famous photo in physics was a misplaced star.

items.title: The Falling Lift
items.question: You float inside a freely falling lift. Which experiment could reveal you're falling, not drifting in deep space?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Einstein's happiest thought: gravity vanishes inside a falling room.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: none — free fall feels weightless. No local test separates free fall from deep-space drift. The principle extends: acceleration mimics gravity everywhere. Elevators, rockets and orbits all trade on the confusion.
items.lessonContent:
Einstein's happiest thought: gravity vanishes inside a falling room.
No local test separates free fall from deep-space drift.
The principle extends: acceleration mimics gravity everywhere.
Elevators, rockets and orbits all trade on the confusion.
Share this: explain tonight why astronauts float though gravity still grips them.

items.title: Climbing Light
items.question: Light escaping a massive star shifts toward which end of the spectrum?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — photons pay for altitude with energy, arriving redder than they left.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: red — it loses energy climbing. Pound and Rebka measured the shift across a mere building. GPS and cosmology both correct for the climb daily. Downhill light gains the same energy back, bluer.
items.lessonContent:
Photons pay for altitude with energy — redder means poorer.
Pound and Rebka measured the shift across a mere building.
GPS and cosmology both correct for the climb daily.
Downhill light gains the same energy back, bluer.
Share this: tell someone starlight arrives tired.

items.title: Bent Starlight
items.question: Massive galaxy clusters smear background galaxies into glowing arcs. What bends that light?
items.correctExplanation: Right — massive foregrounds warp the space behind them into lenses.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the cluster's gravity. Mass warps nearby spacetime, and light follows the warp into arcs and rings. Lensing weighs invisible dark matter by its bending. Astronomy now maps the unseen with borrowed light.
items.lessonContent:
Massive foregrounds warp the space behind them into lenses.
Einstein rings are the perfect-alignment special case.
Lensing weighs invisible dark matter by its bending.
Astronomy now maps the unseen with borrowed light.
Share this: look through a wine glass base tonight for a tabletop lens.

items.title: Plane Clocks
items.question: Hafele and Keating flew atomic clocks around the world in 1971. What did the reunited clocks show?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — eastbound lost time, westbound gained; motion and altitude pulling opposite ways, motion winning overall.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: the flying clocks aged less. Two airliners carried cesium hearts east and west. Eastbound lost time, westbound gained — motion and altitude pulling opposite ways. The measured offsets matched relativity's ledger.
items.lessonContent:
Two airliners carried cesium hearts east and west.
Eastbound lost time, westbound gained — motion and altitude pulling opposite ways.
The measured offsets matched relativity's ledger.
Aviation-grade proof you can board.
Share this: explain tonight that frequent flyers are microseconds younger.

items.title: Timeless Photons
items.question: From light's own 'perspective', how much time passes on its journey?
items.correctExplanation: Right — push the equations to light speed and proper time collapses to zero.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: none at all. Photons do not age; emission and absorption touch with nothing between. Only massless things ride this edge — everything else pays in time. 'Perspective' is metaphor: no frame exists at light speed.
items.lessonContent:
Push the equations to light speed and proper time collapses to zero.
Photons do not age; emission and absorption touch with nothing between.
Only massless things ride this edge — everything else pays in time.
'Perspective' is metaphor: no frame exists at light speed.
Share this: tell someone starlight arrives newborn no matter the distance.

items.title: Stretched Travelers
items.question: What happens to astronauts falling feet-first into a stellar black hole?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — gravity gradients pull feet harder than head; the difference grows lethal.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: tidal forces stretch them thin. Popular accounts call the fate spaghettification. Small holes kill before the horizon; giant ones defer it. Inside, the singularity waits in every future.
items.lessonContent:
Gravity gradients pull feet harder than head — the difference grows lethal.
Popular accounts call the fate by a pasta name.
Small holes kill before the horizon; giant ones defer it.
Inside, the singularity waits in every future.
Share this: explain tonight why falling feet-first is the worst orientation.

items.title: The Fitting Ladder
items.question: A ladder moving near light speed fits inside a shorter barn — yet riders aboard insist it cannot. Who is right?
items.correctExplanation: Right — length contraction squeezes the moving ladder in the barn's books, while simultaneity of the doors differs aboard.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: both — simultaneity splits the verdict. Whether both doors ever shut together depends on the frame's simultaneity. No contradiction survives once 'at the same time' is indexed. Length contraction and door-timing conspire consistently.
items.lessonContent:
Length contraction squeezes the moving ladder in the barn's books.
Aboard, the barn squeezes instead — motion is mutual.
Whether both doors ever shut together depends on the frame's simultaneity.
No contradiction survives once 'at the same time' is indexed.
Share this: ask someone if a fast ladder fits a short barn — then ask 'says who?'.

items.title: Snapping String
items.question: Two rockets tied by a string accelerate identically side by side. What happens to the string?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — identical acceleration preserves separation in the launch frame only; rigidity fails across frames.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: it stretches then snaps. Each rocket's own rulers shrink the gap's measure differently — rigidity fails. Bell designed it to break intuition about 'moving together'. Born-rigid motion is far stricter than matched throttles.
items.lessonContent:
Identical acceleration preserves separation in the launch frame only.
Each rocket's own rulers shrink the gap's measure differently — rigidity fails.
Bell designed it to break intuition about 'moving together'.
Born-rigid motion is far stricter than matched throttles.
Share this: ask tonight why two matched rockets can't share a tow rope.
